title: Speech during the courtesy visit to the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC)
platform: Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Abuja
body:
PROTOCOL

The Chairman of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission, Dr. Musa Adamu Aliyu, SAN; distinguished members of the ICPC Board; the Secretary to the Commission; Directors and Management Staff — I bring warm greetings from the National Executive Council and the over 10,000 members of the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors.

1. INTRODUCTION

It is an honour to lead this delegation to your Commission today. We are grateful for the warm reception and for accommodating this visit at short notice. Our letter requesting this audience was written in April, and we appreciate the Chairman's prompt response in granting it.

The NIQS and the ICPC share a common thread — integrity, transparency, and accountability. These are not merely professional obligations; they are the values upon which our collective service to Nigeria rests. Our presence here today reaffirms that shared commitment and our determination to deepen it.

2. COMMENDING THE ICPC

Mr. Chairman, the ICPC has demonstrated, through sustained and measurable action, that corruption can be confronted. In 2025 alone, the Commission recovered over ₦37 billion and $2.35 million, investigated 263 cases, and achieved a conviction rate exceeding 55%. These outcomes affirm that the institutions established to protect Nigeria's public resources are equal to their mandate.

We also note with pride Nigeria's recent exit from the FATF grey list — a milestone in which the ICPC's strategic leadership played a significant role. The NIQS congratulates the Commission and recognises it as evidence that sustained institutional integrity produces results beyond our borders.

3. THE ANTI-CORRUPTION ACADEMY OF NIGERIA (ACAN)

Mr. Chairman, enforcement alone cannot transform a nation. The establishment of ACAN reflects the ICPC's recognition that lasting change requires the deliberate cultivation of integrity across institutions and professional communities.

NIQS strongly identifies with this philosophy. We are pleased to report that the President of NIQS has already received in audience the Provost of ACAN, and that the Institute is actively planning to participate in ACAN's training program scheduled for 28th-30th April, 2026. We look forward to taking part in this important capacity-building initiative, themed "Achieving Zero Tolerance for Corruption in the Workplace: Anti-Corruption, Ethics and Integrity." This is not merely institutional courtesy — it is a concrete step towards embedding anti-corruption values within the built environment profession.

We see ACAN as a natural partner, particularly for training procurement officers, project managers, and public officials on construction economics, cost transparency, and professional ethics in infrastructure delivery.

4. SEVEN YEARS OF COLLABORATION: THE CEPTG

Mr. Chairman, our formal engagement with the ICPC dates to April 2015. From the Code of Professional Practice deliberations to the 2017 Colloquium with Business Management Organisations and Professional Associations, to the launch of the Constituency and Executive Projects Tracking Group — CEPTG — in 2019, NIQS has been a consistent and committed partner.

For seven years, our members have worked alongside ICPC teams across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones, providing technical expertise in cost verification, project valuation, forensic quantity surveying, and physical site monitoring. The outcomes have been nationally significant:

• Cost Savings: The identification of inflated contract sums and detection of substandard work have safeguarded public resources amounting to trillions of naira, as reflected in ICPC's published reports.

• Project Delivery: Abandoned projects — schools, health centres, water schemes, and road networks — were compelled to completion, delivering real dividends to communities that had given up hope.

• Public Confidence: Transparent, professional monitoring has demonstrated that government projects can be accountably delivered when institutions collaborate with purpose.

The most recent phase — the Special Tracking Exercise, launched in November 2025 and covering 760 federal road projects with a combined value exceeding ₦36 trillion — is the most ambitious expression of this partnership to date. NIQS members are deployed alongside ICPC investigators and Ministry of Works engineers across all 36 states and the FCT. We are proud to be part of it.

5. FORMALISING AND EXPANDING THE PARTNERSHIP

Mr. Chairman, seven years of pro bono service by our members — Fellows and corporate members with active professional practices — is a testament to their patriotism. But as the scale and complexity of these assignments have grown, so too has the need for a sustainable institutional framework.

We therefore formally propose the conclusion of a Memorandum of Understanding between NIQS and the ICPC. The MOU would: (i) institutionalise the collaboration with a clear legal and operational framework that endures beyond individual administrations; (ii) ensure professional remuneration, transitioning from voluntary service to structured compensation that enables NIQS to consistently deploy its most experienced professionals; (iii) enhance capacity building through joint training, research, and knowledge exchange in project auditing, procurement monitoring, and forensic cost analysis; and (iv) expand preventive oversight by involving NIQS members at the planning and procurement stages, where corruption risks are highest.

Beyond formalising existing work, we also wish to propose two additional areas where NIQS expertise can directly strengthen the ICPC's transparency mandate.

The first is the adoption of the International Cost Management Standards (ICMS) for reporting construction costs on public projects. Currently, the absence of uniform cost reporting standards in Nigeria makes it difficult to compare contract sums, benchmark project costs, or reliably detect inflation. ICMS provides a globally recognised framework that brings consistency, comparability, and credibility to how construction costs are classified and reported. Its adoption on public projects would give the ICPC and oversight agencies a far sharper instrument for identifying anomalies and holding contractors accountable.

The second is the adoption of unified standards for the measurement of construction quantities and the preparation of Bills of Quantities (BOQs). In the absence of a single national standard, different consultants and contractors prepare BOQs using different methodologies, making it almost impossible to conduct reliable cost audits or detect fraudulent misrepresentation of quantities. The NIQS is best placed to lead the development and promotion of a unified Nigerian measurement standard, and we respectfully propose that the ICPC formally supports and endorses this initiative as a tool for procurement transparency.

Together, these two proposals represent a shift from reactive detection to proactive prevention — building the technical infrastructure that makes corruption in construction contracts harder to commit and easier to detect.

6. CONCLUSION

Mr. Chairman, before we conclude, permit us a brief word about who we are — because it speaks directly to why this partnership matters. We say this with a smile, because we are aware that even among the most learned in our society, the Quantity Surveyor is sometimes confused with the Land Surveyor. We assure you, Mr. Chairman, we do not carry theodolites or measure plots of land. What we measure is far more consequential to the national treasury — we measure costs. And if you will permit a legal analogy, Mr. Chairman: just as a Senior Advocate ensures that justice is not miscarried in the courtroom, the Quantity Surveyor ensures that value is not miscarried on the construction site.

The Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors is Nigeria's foremost cost management professional body, with thousands of members trained in the full economics of construction — from project inception through procurement to final account. Our profession operates at the intersection of cost, procurement, and contract administration — the very points where value is either protected or lost. It is no accident, therefore, that when the ICPC needed professional eyes on Nigeria's public infrastructure, it turned to Quantity Surveyors. We are, by training and calling, guardians of value for money.

We are confident today that this visit will mark the beginning of a deeper, more formalized, and more impactful phase of our collaboration. The NIQS is ready. Our members are committed. And Nigeria deserves no less.

On behalf of the National Executive Council and the membership of the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors, I thank you sincerely, Mr. Chairman, for this audience.

God bless the ICPC. God bless the NIQS. And God bless the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

title: Speech during the courtesy visit to the Fiscal Responsibility Commission (FRC)
platform: Fiscal Responsibility Commission (FRC), Abuja — courtesy visit and MOU signing
body:
PROTOCOL

The Acting Chairman of the Fiscal Responsibility Commission, Mr. Charles Chukwuemeka Abana; distinguished members of the Commission's leadership; the Secretary to the Commission; Directors and Management Staff — I bring warm greetings from the National Executive Council and the over 10,000 members of the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors.

1. APPRECIATION

It is a privilege to lead this delegation to your Commission today, and we are grateful for the warmth of your reception.

Mr. Acting Chairman, the relationship between NIQS and the Fiscal Responsibility Commission is one we hold in deep regard. It is a relationship built on a shared conviction — that public resources must be managed with discipline, transparency, and professional rigour. Our first formal MOU, executed on 22nd October 2021, gave institutional expression to that conviction. Today, we are here to renew and deepen it.

We also take this opportunity to acknowledge the Commission's strong institutional track record in advancing fiscal discipline and accountability across Nigeria's public sector. That legacy of commitment is what makes this partnership meaningful, and what gives us confidence in the work ahead.

2. WHAT QUANTITY SURVEYORS BRING TO FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY

Mr. Acting Chairman, permit me a brief word about who we are and why this partnership matters.

The Quantity Surveyor is Nigeria's foremost construction cost manager. From project conception through procurement, contract administration, and final account, we operate at the precise intersection where public money is either protected or lost. We measure costs. We verify values. We detect inflation. And where contracts have been manipulated, we provide the forensic evidence that accountability requires.

The FRC's mandate — ensuring that public expenditure is prudent, transparent, and consistent with Nigeria's fiscal framework — cannot be fully discharged without professional cost intelligence on capital projects. That is precisely what NIQS provides. Our collaboration is therefore not a matter of institutional convenience. It is a functional necessity.

3. OUR CONTINUED COMMITMENT

We are here today to reaffirm NIQS's unwavering commitment to supporting the Commission's mandate. In the renewed MOU we present for execution today, we propose a strengthened framework that reflects the maturity of our partnership and the growing demands of Nigeria's infrastructure oversight environment.

Key elements of the renewed collaboration include:

• Joint Physical Verification Exercises of capital projects — ensuring that what is reported in MDA budgets and expenditure returns reflects what is actually on the ground;

• Forensic cost auditing to detect contract inflation, value misrepresentation, and procurement irregularities;

• Pre-appropriation cost advisory, embedding NIQS expertise at the budget preparation and MTEF review stages where fiscal risks are highest; and

• Joint reporting that gives the Commission technically credible, professionally prepared outputs suitable for enforcement and accountability purposes.

We also propose the establishment of a Joint Implementation Committee to give the partnership its own governance architecture — ensuring continuity, structured engagement, and mutual accountability regardless of changes in leadership on either side.

4. CAPACITY BUILDING THROUGH THE QSA

Mr. Acting Chairman, knowledge is the foundation of effective oversight. The NIQS Quantity Surveyors Academy — our dedicated capacity building platform — is available to the Commission for the training of FRC staff in specialised knowledge areas including construction economics, capital project cost management, procurement integrity, and the forensic analysis of infrastructure expenditure.

We propose that this be formalised under the renewed MOU, so that FRC personnel are equipped with the technical tools necessary to interrogate capital project claims with professional confidence. An oversight body that understands cost is an oversight body that cannot easily be misled.

5. STANDARDS ADVOCACY — A SHARED FRONTIER

We also wish to flag two technical proposals that will directly strengthen the Commission's oversight capacity.

The first is the adoption of the International Cost Management Standards (ICMS) for reporting construction costs on public projects — bringing consistency, comparability, and credibility to how capital expenditure is classified and reported across MDAs.

The second is the development of a Unified National Standard for Bills of Quantities (BOQ) — eliminating the measurement inconsistencies that currently make reliable cost auditing extremely difficult.

These are not academic proposals. They are practical tools that will make fiscal irresponsibility in capital projects harder to commit and easier to detect. We invite the Commission's formal endorsement and advocacy support for both.

6. CONCLUSION

Mr. Acting Chairman, the Nigerian taxpayer deserves institutions that work together in their defence. The NIQS and the FRC share that calling. Our renewed MOU is not merely a document — it is a renewed covenant to serve Nigeria with professionalism and purpose.

We are ready to sign, and we are ready to work.

On behalf of the National Executive Council and the membership of the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors, I thank you sincerely for this audience.

God bless the Fiscal Responsibility Commission. God bless the NIQS. And God bless the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

title: Goodwill address during the courtesy visit to the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP)
platform: Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), The Presidency, Abuja
body:
PROTOCOL

The Director-General, Distinguished Management and Staff of the Bureau of Public Procurement, My Colleagues on the Council of the Institute, Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen.

It is a great honour to lead the delegation of the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors on this courtesy visit to the Bureau of Public Procurement. We come, first and foremost, to pay our respects to a distinguished reformer and an Honorary Fellow of our Institute, and to reaffirm the Institute's firm and unreserved support for the reform agenda you are driving with such energy and conviction.

A REFORMER OF RARE ENERGY AND VISION

Director-General, permit me to say plainly what the entire built-environment community has come to recognise: yours has been a tenure of extraordinary pace and purpose. In recent days alone, the record speaks for itself. Only this week, on the 13th of July, you unveiled the National Guidelines for Public Procurement of Food and Related Services — a landmark framework ensuring that public spending on food in our schools, hospitals and correctional centres delivers genuine value for money while safeguarding nutrition, food safety and public health.

Days earlier, you sat with the Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the heads of our sister anti-corruption agencies to forge a stronger inter-agency framework against corruption — anchored on a principle we find compelling: that the most effective anti-corruption strategy is to design procurement systems that prevent corruption before it occurs, rather than to pursue wrongdoing after the fact. Given that procurement and contract fraud account for the overwhelming share of public-sector corruption, this preventive philosophy is, in our respectful view, exactly the right one.

And these are but moments in a relentless schedule. Days earlier still, you carried Nigeria's voice to the continental stage — at the Regional Workshop on Electronic Government Procurement in Zambia, convened by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime with the Open Contracting Partnership — advancing the transparent, digital procurement systems that Africa's future demands. And only last weekend in Ikot Ekpene, you convened the Federal Permanent Secretaries — our nation's Accounting Officers — and reminded them that "a budget is a covenant with the people, and procurement leadership is how we keep that covenant." It was there that the Bureau reported a remarkable achievement: savings of approximately ₦1.1 trillion for the Federal Government in 2025, driven by improved price intelligence and budget evaluation. Director-General, permit us to observe that price intelligence and budget evaluation are, at their heart, cost management — the very discipline our profession exists to serve. That your Bureau now marches to an anthem titled "Value for Money Always" tells us we speak, already, the same language.

We salute this energy. We salute this vision. And we are proud that a reformer of this calibre wears the honour of our Fellowship.

REFORM ANCHORED ON VALUE FOR MONEY

What draws the Quantity Surveying profession so naturally to your reform agenda is its central organising idea — value for money. Your recent Guidelines on the Revised Policy for Variations of Contract Sums and the Mandatory Use of Final Designs of 14th May 2026 address the very heart of what has long troubled public infrastructure delivery: excessive variations, weak design coordination, poorly documented fluctuation claims, and the cost overruns that flow from them.

We wish to place on record that the Institute supports this policy direction. The insistence on final designs before award, the clear distinction between variation and fluctuation claims, and the demand that such claims be handled — in the words of the Circular itself — professionally, are principles our profession has advocated for decades. They are, quite simply, sound cost management.

We are equally encouraged by your vision of sector-based procurement and your call for professionals across every sector to be equipped with procurement competence. If food procurement now has its dedicated guidelines, we are confident — and we respectfully anticipate — that the procurement of works and construction will receive the same considered, sector-specific attention. Indeed, through the Variations and Fluctuations policy, you have already begun that journey.

COMING AS PARTNERS IN COST MANAGEMENT

Director-General, we come not to petition, but to partner. The Quantity Surveyor is, by statutory mandate and professional training, Nigeria's Cost Management Professional — the specialist in measurement, cost planning, valuation, variation analysis, fluctuation assessment and the final account. These are precisely the disciplines on which your Variations Circular depends, from the Bill of Quantities to interim valuations and the derivation of fluctuation claims from the Schedule of Rates. Where public money is measured, valued and safeguarded, that is the work of the Cost Management Professional.

This is not a parochial claim; it is a global standard. The World Bank's own procurement guidance on Value for Money and Price Benchmarking, the work of the International Monetary Fund, and the International Cost Management Standard (ICMS) now treat rigorous, independent cost management as essential to sound public finance — and name the Cost Management Professional as the competent custodian of that function. Nigeria already has this profession, established and regulated by statute. We should be glad, in the course of our engagement, to share with the Bureau our Standard Methods of Measurement and the ICMS framework, as practical instruments to strengthen the very objectives your reforms pursue.

We are grateful, too, for the confidence the Bureau has already shown the Institute — through our participation in your Consultative Meetings with Contractors and Stakeholders in Kano and Lagos, and through your invitation to nominate a member to the National Procurement Strategy Development Committee. We stand ready to take up that role fully, and to place the technical capacity of our membership at the service of your reforms.

A SHARED INTEREST IN A COHERENT PROFESSIONAL FRAMEWORK

Director-General, this visit itself arose from your gracious invitation to our Institute in the matter presently before the Federal High Court. We are grateful for that confidence, and we see in it a wider opportunity — to reflect together on how Nigeria's several statutory professional and procurement frameworks may operate in harmonious coexistence, each within its lawful mandate, rather than in overlap or contest.

We raise, in the same collaborative spirit, a matter we believe is of shared concern: the growing proliferation of bodies laying claim to aspects of procurement practice in our country. Where mandates blur, the risks are precisely those your reforms seek to eliminate — duplication, uncertainty, and diminished accountability. As the Regulator, the Bureau is uniquely placed to ensure that this landscape remains coherent, and that the distinct statutory competencies of the established professions — the Quantity Surveyor's role as Nigeria's Cost Management Professional among them — are recognised and preserved within it. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss this further with the Bureau.

CONCLUSION

Director-General, the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors offers you today its hand in genuine partnership. Your goals are our goals: transparency, accountability, probity and value for money in the expenditure of public resources. Where you seek to protect the public purse, you will find in the Quantity Surveying profession a willing, capable and statutorily grounded ally.

We commend your giant strides, we affirm our institutional support, and we look forward to a long and productive collaboration in the service of our nation.

God bless the BPP, God bless the NIQS. And God bless the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

title: Address during the courtesy visit to the National Universities Commission (NUC)
body:
PROTOCOL

The Executive Secretary, Directors and Management Staff of the Commission; Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen.

It is a privilege to stand before you this afternoon. On behalf of the Council and the entire membership of the Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors, I thank you, Executive Secretary, for receiving us. The Commission is the custodian of standards for our university system, and it is in that spirit of shared responsibility for quality that we have come.

The Nigerian Institute of Quantity Surveyors is the professional home of the Quantity Surveyor — the cost manager of the built environment, whose work secures value for money on every naira of public and private construction expenditure. Our regulatory arm, the Quantity Surveyors Registration Board of Nigeria (QSRBN), established by Cap Q1, Laws of the Federation, carries the statutory mandate for the training, registration and discipline of the profession. It is on a matter that unites the Commission's mandate and the Board's that we seek your partnership today.

Executive Secretary, we come with a single, focused proposal — that the Commission and the Board formalise their collaboration through a Memorandum of Understanding, anchored on four objectives:

1. JOINT ACCREDITATION
That the accreditation of university programmes in Quantity Surveying be conducted jointly by the NUC and the QSRBN, so that academic approval and professional recognition move as one, and our graduates emerge both qualified and registrable.

2. STANDARDS AND CURRICULUM
That we work together to set and periodically review the minimum academic standards and curriculum for the discipline, keeping the Nigerian Quantity Surveyor abreast of global practice in cost management, procurement and digital delivery.

3. DEEPENING COLLABORATION BETWEEN PRACTICE AND ACADEMIA
That collaborative partnership deliberately bridges the classroom and the field — embedding the practitioner's experience into curriculum development and delivery, so that what is taught reflects what the profession truly requires. Similarly, the academia will conduct research on industry problems and provide pragmatic solutions for the development of the built environment.

These, Executive Secretary, are not competing mandates but complementary ones. The Commission assures the standard of the degree; the Board assures the standard of the professional. Where the two are joined, the nation is the beneficiary — in better-trained graduates, stronger institutions, and the prudent stewardship of public resources that quality quantity surveying makes possible. We are encouraged, too, that our two constituencies already share common ground through the SPESSE initiative, and we see this partnership as a natural next step.

We therefore respectfully seek the Commission's partnership in bringing this Memorandum of Understanding to fruition and stand ready to work with your Directorate of Accreditation at your convenience. I thank you most sincerely for your audience.

God bless the NUC, God bless the NIQS. And God bless the Federal Republic of Nigeria.
